records.quote:
Again the lightning flashed--but this time upon a scene not wholly
strange. It was Greenwich, the Greenwich that used to be
records.paraphrase: A second vision shows an earlier version of Greenwich.

records.quote:
"Good God!" I whispered; "can you do that for _any time_?" And as he
nodded
records.paraphrase: The host confirms he can display any period of time through the window.

records.quote:
a flash of heat-lightning played
over the scene, and I looked out upon a sea of luxuriant
foliage--foliage unpolluted, and not the sea of roofs to be expected
by any normal mind.
records.paraphrase: Through the window the narrator sees a past landscape of foliage instead of the modern city.

records.quote:
The steep street of my approach was nowhere
visible, and the little I did see succumbed rapidly to a mist that
rolled in from the river despite the glaring moonlight.
records.paraphrase: The street by which the narrator arrived has disappeared, leaving unfamiliar surroundings.

records.quote:
It spread over the old man, too, whether from the
same source or because of his fear and vehemence, and I saw him
shrivel and blacken as he lurched near and strove to rend me with
vulturine talons.
records.paraphrase: The old man shrivels and blackens under the moonlight.

records.quote:
this city of stone and stridor is not
a sentient perpetuation of Old New York as London is of Old London and
Paris of Old Paris, but that it is in fact quite dead, its sprawling
body imperfectly embalmed and infested with queer animate things
records.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts New York with London and Paris, claiming it is dead and infested rather than a living continuation.

records.quote:
The squire who
succeeded to it in 1768 studied sartain arts and made sartain
discoveries, all connected with influences residing in this particular
plot of ground, and eminently desarving of the strongest guarding.
records.paraphrase: The host explains that an ancestor made discoveries tied to powers residing in this specific plot of ground.

records.quote:
at the first touch of his
ungloved fingers I turned cold. His flesh, though dry and firm, was of
the quality of ice
records.paraphrase: The narrator reacts with a chill upon touching the host's icy flesh.

records.quote:
reports could state no more than that I had appeared from
a place unknown, at the entrance of a little black court off Perry
Street.
records.paraphrase: The narrator is found emerging from an unknown place, the site of his ordeal unlocatable.

records.quote:
I saw the heavens verminous with strange flying things,
and beneath them a hellish black city of giant stone terraces with
impious pyramids flung savagely to the moon, and devil-lights burning
from unnumbered windows.
records.paraphrase: A vision of a monstrous future city with flying things and towering terraces.

records.quote:
Thereafter he bargained
with them and exchanged the free access of his grounds for the exact
inwardness of what they did; larning that their grandfathers got part
of their custom from red ancestors and part from an old Dutchman in
the time of the States-General.
records.paraphrase: The ancestor investigated the Indians' rites by bargaining for and learning their secret practices and origins.

records.quote:
the door fell in
pieces to admit a colossal, shapeless influx of inky substance starred
with shining, malevolent eyes.
records.paraphrase: A shapeless black mass full of eyes bursts into the room.

records.quote:
forgetting every injunction to silence I
screamed and screamed and screamed as my nerves gave way and the walls
quivered about me.
records.paraphrase: The narrator screams uncontrollably in terror at the future vision.

candidate.quote:
there appeared to reside some
very remarkable qualities in the will of mankind; qualities having a
little-suspected dominance not only over the acts of one
s self and of
others, but over every variety of force and substance in Nature, and
over many elements and dimensions deemed more universal than Nature
herself.
candidate.paraphrase: The host describes a claimed power of human will to dominate forces, substances, and dimensions of nature.

candidate.quote:
all the world is but the smoke of our intellects; past
the bidding of the vulgar, but by the wise to be puffed out and drawn
in like any cloud of prime Virginia tobacco. What we want, we may make
about us; and what we don	 want, we may sweep away.
candidate.paraphrase: The host explains a theory that the world can be shaped and dismissed by the intellect of the wise.

criteria.rationale: The host frames his ancestor's power over space, time, and Nature as 'arts and discoveries' connected to influences in the ground, but this is presented as occult necromancy rather than materially represented science. The pseudo-scientific framing is decorative rather than a genuine scientific fact or process.

No engineered device, invention, or technique materially drives the story. The window visions are produced by magical gesture and will, not by any device or engineered system. Candles, lanterns, and keys are ordinary period objects.

The window reveals a remote past landscape of primeval foliage, an earlier Greenwich, and a monstrous far-future city; the host confirms he can display 'any time.' These temporal displacements of vista are central to the story's climax.

The narrator's premise that the city is dead and 'infested' is developed into a horrific future vision of a degenerate stone city, a loose extrapolation of urban dread. However, this is more atmospheric prophecy than consequence systematically developed from an identifiable premise.

The ancestor bargained with and learned the Indians' secret rites, but this is acquisitive inquiry into occult lore, not observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or evidential revision. No systematic scientific method materially drives understanding or action.

The future vision shows heavens 'verminous with strange flying things' and a nonordinary cosmic-horror cityscape, and a colossal shapeless influx of inky substance starred with malevolent eyes intrudes
delivering a substantially nonordinary presence. These constitute nonordinary environments/visitors.

The old man shrivels and blackens and a monstrous black mass overwhelms him amid the collapsing house. This is a localized supernatural destruction of a single man and building rather than a large-scale disaster, so materiality and scale for catastrophe are uncertain.

candidates.description: The necromancer's window/apparatus that displays and seemingly manifests any period of time (past pastoral Greenwich, transitional Greenwich, and a monstrous far-future city), grounded in the ancestor's 'arts and discoveries' concerning powers residing in this plot of ground and a will-based metaphysics that treats space and time as pliable.

novelty.rationale: The power to reveal/manifest any time through the window is a world-altering difference from the empirical norm, but it is presented as a localized occult 'spectacle' rather than a totalizing transformation of the story universe, so novelty is partial/ambiguous.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The account is explicitly framed as 'sartain arts,' necromancy, Indian rites, and 'powers,' with retributive supernatural vengeance (the black influx, the shriveling old man). It rests on magic and the supernatural rather than a coherent, systematic, immanent nonsupernatural logic, so cognitive validation is absent.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The window and the temporal visions drive the central encounter and its horrific climax; the narrator's scream at the future vision precipitates the catastrophe, so the device governs the overriding narrative logic.

estrangement.rationale: The pastoral past and monstrous future glimpsed through the window contrast sharply with the narrator's modern New York, dislocating both reader and narrator, but the mechanism is occult rather than cognitively rationalized.

candidates.description: The ice-fleshed, centuries-old necromancer who has preserved his ancestral seat and his own longevity through occult arts, ultimately destroyed by the returning dead Indians' supernatural vengeance.

novelty.rationale: An unnaturally long-lived, ice-cold being is a striking departure from the norm, but it is a single uncanny individual rather than a world-altering condition.

cognitive_validation.rationale: His longevity and destruction are explained by magic and supernatural retribution, not by any immanent nonsupernatural system.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: He is the story's central figure, but the governing engine of the plot is the temporal-vision demonstration and its consequences, of which he is the operator.

estrangement.rationale: The ice-quality flesh and archaic costume estrange the reader, signaling something beyond mortal norms, yet framed as supernatural.
